ethics_check.summary_text: 1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Due to the quotas assigned by Qualtrics, the participants were skewed toward the 25-34 and 55-65 age groups compared to the U.S. population reported by the 2022 United States Census Bureau (U.S. Census Bureau, 2022, Table S0101).

table.text: The California Institute of Integral Studies Human Research and Review Committee approved the experimental procedures, and participants provided written informed consent.
Participants were informed that the study investigated the feeling of connection, but not that it also examined differences in head and heart self-location areas.
Participants were asked to click in one of these areas to indicate where they felt their sense of self was located at that moment (state), and this click was recorded as a point in the body outline.

Participants were informed that the study would examine the nature of a strong feeling of connection with others (as in emotional connection, rather than erotic or sexual touch connection) and investigate what it means to engage with the world from a state of connectedness.
Participants were 107 female, 110 male, and 1 intersex; mean age 47 (25-65).
Fourth, although participants were deliberately kept unaware that the study examined self-location, reducing demand characteristics, these cannot be fully eliminated in a self-report design.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: A power analysis using the G*Power app determined the sample size, indicating that two groups of 105 participants each would require an effect size of Cohen's d = 0.5, thereby allowing the use of p-values in hypothesis testing. SPSS v.27 was used for data analyses. The SELF, MPS, SCS, WCS, IOS, and QCM assessments were subjected to Pearson correlations and one-way ANOVA (i.e., t-tests), which allowed us to control for other variables (e.g., age, education) and assess validity. False Discovery Rate (FDR)-adjusted Benjamini-Hochberg p-value at a q < .05 level of false discovery rate-was applied post hoc to control for the elevated risk of type I error rates associated with conducting multiple comparisons. The FDR is reported as q-value. The SP Body Map was analyzed by performing a chi-square test. A post hoc ANOVA test was performed for analysis of the nine qualities of connection included in the DSLQ.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Participants were asked to click in one of these areas to indicate where they felt their sense of self was located at that moment (state), and this click was recorded as a point in the body outline.

Participants were informed that the study would examine the nature of a strong feeling of connection with others (as in emotional connection, rather than erotic or sexual touch connection) and investigate what it means to engage with the world from a state of connectedness.
Participants were 107 female, 110 male, and 1 intersex; mean age 47 (25-65).

text.text: Research has typically examined how self-location in the head or heart is associated with traits and behavior, yet its link to relationality-specifically the felt sense of connectionremains underexplored.
This study investigated how dispositional self-location predicts the embodied experience of being relationally linked to others and the world.
We initially developed the Dispositional Self-Location Questionnaire (DSLQ), an association-based instrument designed to minimize potential subjective bias in participant reporting of self-location.

Using this measure, we categorized a U.S. sample of 218 adults who had reported a strong experience of connection as head-locators or heart-locators and assessed them on self-construal, selfexpansiveness, connectedness, and perceived qualities of connection.
Head-locators reported firmer self-boundaries, emphasizing independence, rationality, and decision-making.

In contrast, Heart-locators scored significantly higher on connectedness to both self and world, and on metapersonal self-construal, describing their connections as close, warm, caring, and authentic.

These findings suggest that self-location functions as a somatic attentional stance that anticipates the experiential boundary between self and other: the head favors separation and autonomy, while the heart favors openness and expanded belonging.

Across cultures and generations, poets, mystics, and lovers have reported warm sensations of expansion in the heart area, as if there were a presence radiating out to bond with another, with nature, or with the world itself.

Beyond metaphor, these descriptions closely resemble what Yaden et al. (2017) describe as self-transcendent experiences, particularly forms of relational self-transcendence marked by softened self-boundaries, heightened warmth, and a vivid sense of unity with others.

(2017)</ref> describe as self-transcendent experiences, particularly forms of relational self-transcendence marked by softened self-boundaries, heightened warmth, and a vivid sense of unity with others.

text.text: Self-transcendent experiences are temporary mental states of "decreased self-salience and increased feelings of connectedness" (Yaden et al., 2017, p. 1).

text.text: Because these experiences are frequently reported as centered in the chest, they suggest that selflocation-especially heart-location-may shape relational openness.

This aligns with phenomenological accounts suggesting that the felt sense of connection is a bodily experience of relatedness, belonging, and interconnectedness rooted in the body's intertwining with the world (Merleau-Ponty, 2013).
text.formatted: This aligns with phenomenological accounts suggesting that the felt sense of connection is a bodily experience of relatedness, belonging, and interconnectedness rooted in the body's intertwining with the world <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Merleau-Ponty, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, variations in self-location may have direct implications for relational experience.
Yet despite its significance in human experience, the phenomenon of felt connection has received limited empirical attention.
The self, embodied and intertwined with the environment, extends beyond conceptual representation (Oyserman, 2001) and is grounded in lived experience (James, 1890).

text.text: It shapes a first-person perspective-the phenomenal self -as an experiential position from which one perceives the world (Braun et al., 2018), anchored in pre-reflective interactions (Gendlin, 1999).

text.text: Along with detecting the surrounding world, the self is modulated by core visceral physiological signals (Damasio & Damasio, 2023).

text.text: The perception of these signals, labeled interoception, configures self-conceptions and helps stabilize the self over time.
Among all organs, the heart, along with the lungs, has been shown to provide substantial visceral input (Monti et al., 2021).

text.text: Interoceptive accuracy modulates social and emotional processing and helps establish self-other boundaries, with direct consequences for relational capacities (Von Mohr et al., 2021).

text.text: Within subjective experience, some bodily areas are more closely associated with the self than others (Howard & Templeton, 1966). Seih and Lepicovsky (2020) defined it as the organ or bodily site where the sense of "I" is perceived to reside.

text.text: The concept of self-construal assesses an individual's self-image, reflecting the cognitive and emotional aspects of their identity.
Traditionally, individual selfconstrual was categorized as either independent (distinct and unique) or interdependent (interpersonally connected; Singelis, 1994).

text.text: Later, a third dimension was added: the metapersonal self-construal (DeCicco & Stroink, 2007), defined as a stable self-understanding in which the self is experienced as profoundly interconnected with all humanity and nature-not merely with close others, but with a wider relational field that includes the non-human world.

text.text: It also differs from universality orientation, which centers on spiritual or mystical identification with the cosmos (Cloninger et al., 1994); the metapersonal self does not require a spiritual framework but instead extends the scope of relational self-construal beyond the interpersonal to include connection to nature and the world.

text.text: This distinction matters because mainstream social psychology has traditionally defined connection primarily as interpersonal ties (Aron & Aron, 1996), and even when broader connections are acknowledged, they are often minimized or categorized as "spiritual" rather than taken as serious relational phenomena (Baumeister & Leary, 1995).

text.text: Phenomenologically, self-location refers to the location within the body-relative space where attention is interoceptively felt to originate, also termed the egocenter (Hartelius et al., 2022).

text.text: As such, it is distinct from self-concept, which encompasses beliefs and narratives about the self (Gallagher, 2000).

text.text: Neuroscientifically, self-location refers to where one experiences oneself to be localized in space (Ionta et al., 2011, p. 369).

text.text: Evidence suggests that changes in self-location within the body correspond to shifts in cortical activation patterns-particularly in the beta and gamma bands (Hartelius et al., 2022)-and in global cognitive states (Dambrun et al., 2023; Hartelius et al., 2025), indicating that its constructed nature does not diminish its functional reality.

text.text: Recent proposals suggest that self-regulation of the location from which the felt sense of self attends has direct impact on the global cognitive state-a configuration of the cognitive environment such that psychological capacities and resources are prioritized in a specific manner (Hartelius et al., 2023 (Hartelius et al., , 2025)).

text.text: Neurophenomenological studies indicate that the boundaries of the perceived sense of self can soften or dissolve, altering senses of ownership and agency (Ataria et al., 2015; Lindahl et al., 2017; Nave et al., 2021).

text.text: For example, body scan meditation can shift self-perception from a narrative to a minimal self, fostering self-loss, decentering, and a sense of oneness (Dambrun, 2016; Dambrun et al., 2019).

Consistent with this, self-location in the heart area is associated with caring, empathy, emotionality, warmth, intuitive thinking, and happiness, whereas head self-location is associated with knowledge, rationality, and individuality (Dambrun, 2023; Fetterman & Robinson, 2013; Pellerin et al., 2022).

text.text: These associations suggest two relational modes: one oriented toward separation and autonomy, and one toward relational openness and self-transcendence.

While not yet demonstrated, heart-based self-location may also relate more closely to cardiac processes, which convey emotional information to the brain via afferent pathways (Armour, 1991; Lacey & Lacey, 1978).

text.text: Although these findings require cautious interpretation, they underscore the plausibility that heart-centered self-location may predict relational experience.

Most self-location research has traditionally examined its impact on the individual as an egoic entity with defined boundaries, identity, and narrative while overlooking its potential relational implications.
Yet, if the boundaries of the located self can be softened or expanded, then self-location may shape felt connection or separateness.
Additionally, as research has shown, feelings may stem from both rational reasoning and interoceptive perceptions.
As a result, a felt sense of connection can be categorized into at least two types: one rooted in cognitive and rational processes, and the other in somatic and interoceptive experiences.

To date, no research has identified differences in the qualities of connection between cognitive-rooted and interoceptive-rooted feelings, nor has any investigated these differences among head selflocators and heart self-locators.

Because heart self-location is conceptually close to a relational transcendent mode, it seems highly likely that an expansive experience of self-location in the heart area reflects a psychological reality underlying popular notions of a radiant emotional heart.

The present study, therefore, examines whether self-location in the heart area is associated with greater connectedness and less separateness, and identifies qualities associated with relationality, offering an initial empirical investigation of the relational implications of heartbased self-location.

We propose that self-location functions as a somatic attentional stance that anticipates the experiential boundary between self and other: the head fosters separation and autonomy, while the heart fosters openness and expanded belonging.
The present study tests this proposition empirically.

Building on these findings and numerous reports of a recurring sensation of emotional expansion in the heart area across cultures and generations, we designed a cross-sectional, quasiexperimental study using a purposive sample comparing head-locators and heart-locators.

The research question asked how individuals with a heart-located self might differ from those with a head-located self in dimensions of self-concept, self-construal, attentional stance, aspects of connectedness, and qualities of experience associated with an emotional connection to others.
Scores on self-concept, self-construal, and attentional stance were used as context for examining the felt sense of connection.

To improve reliability and reduce conceptual biases inherent in direct self-location inquiries (such as social desirability bias, or biases related to the values and beliefs associated with these highly symbolic and semantically loaded bodily areas) inherent in asking people directly where individuals feel their "I" resides in their bodies, or in asking them to place a dot on a body map as an analogy, we developed an indirect measurement tool: the Dispositional Self-Location Questionnaire (DSLQ).
This association-based approach evaluates links between cognitive or emotional faculties and perceived bodily locations-an assessment previously unavailable.
We hypothesized: • Hypothesis 1: Heart self-locators will report significantly more often self-sensations in the chest area of a visual body map (Attentional Stance) than head self-locators.

• Hypothesis 2: Heart self-locators will score higher on measures of interdependent and metapersonal self-construal, whereas head self-locators will score higher on a measure of independent self-construal.
• Hypothesis 3: Heart self-locators will score higher on the transpersonal subscale of selfexpansiveness (e.g., sense of identity connects to all life through all time and space).
• Hypothesis 4: Heart self-locators will score higher on connectedness to self, others, and world.
• Hypothesis 5: Heart self-locators will rate emotional qualities of connection (warmth, heartfelt) higher than rational qualities (respect, appreciation).

Participants (N = 218) resided in the United States, aged 25-65, fluent in conversational English, not taking psychotropic substances, not diagnosed with a serious psychiatric or neurological disorder, and reporting having experienced a strong emotional connection with another person (or pet).
Participants of any sex, race, educational level, and religious traditions were eligible.
Recruitment was done through Qualtrics® and personal social networks.

Due to the quotas assigned by Qualtrics, the participants were skewed toward the 25-34 and 55-65 age groups compared to the U.S. population reported by the 2022 United States Census Bureau (U.S. Census Bureau, 2022, Table S0101).

Choices of head and heart as focal self-location stem from prior findings indicating individuals commonly associate identity with the head or heart rather than other body parts or external places, at least in a Westernized context and scientific paradigm (Adam et al., 2015; Alsmith & Longo, 2014; Anglin, 2014; Limanowski & Hecht, 2011).

text.text: Participants were informed that the study investigated the feeling of connection, but not that it also examined differences in head and heart self-location areas.
The DSLQ was developed and tested to distinguish between head and heart self-location.
Unlike single-item measures that ask participants to explicitly identify their self-location, the DSLQ mainly uses an indirect, association-based approach.
Aside from one direct question, it triangulates the respondent's dispositional location through cognitive and emotional qualities (Sester, 2024).
text.formatted: Aside from one direct question, it triangulates the respondent's dispositional location through cognitive and emotional qualities <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Sester, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This design minimizes social desirability or conceptual answering (e.g., believing one "should" identify as heart-located) by focusing on felt experience (e.g., "Where in your body do you feel closeness?").

It initially comprised 14 items based on results from relevant studies (Adam et al., 2015; Fetterman & Robinson, 2013), which found associations between cognitive or emotional faculties and head versus heart locations.
text.formatted: It initially comprised 14 items based on results from relevant studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Adam et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Fetterman & Robinson, 2013)</ref>, which found associations between cognitive or emotional faculties and head versus heart locations.

text.text: For each of the items, the maximum score was +1, representing the response expected from a heart-located individual, or -1, representing the response expected from a head-located individual.
Other responses were scored 0.
For example, item 4, a question with four possible answers, asked: "When you feel close to someone, where in your body do you feel the closeness?
Choose one among liver, heart, brain, somewhere else or don't know", for which the score was 0, +1, -1, and 0, respectively.
Validation.
Initial reliability analyses indicated excellent internal consistency for the full 14-item scale (Cronbach's α = .91; McDonald's ω = .91).
However, among the 14 items, four of them had a two-point scale (1, 2), and mixing response formats is not recommended in scale construction.
To ensure conceptual and statistical coherence, we retained the 10 items with uniform three-point response (0, 1, 2; see Appendix A) options and subjected these to Rasch analysis.
Psychometrics.
Rasch analysis of the 10-item scale indicated adequate psychometric quality (see Table S1 in Supplemental Material, appended ).
text.formatted: Rasch analysis of the 10-item scale indicated adequate psychometric quality (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S1</ref> in Supplemental Material, appended ).

text.text: All items demonstrated acceptable model-data fit, with Infit and Outfit values well within recommended thresholds.
Only Item 7 showed a slightly elevated Infit statistic (1.28), which should be monitored in future studies, but did not exceed critical cutoffs.
Item difficulty estimates spanned a broad range (-1.73 to +1.07 logits), ensuring adequate coverage of the latent construct.
Point-biserial correlations were consistently high (.70-.85), confirming that each item contributed meaningfully to the total scale score and that redundancy was minimal.
The measure thus offers a reliable and valid tool for distinguishing between groups.

Attentional stance was measured using a somatic phenomenology body map (SP Body Maps; Hartelius, 2021), a visual analog scale that allows participants to digitally indicate the felt location of their self on a body chart divided into seven zones (head, chest, right arm, left arm, abdomen, pelvis, and legs).
Participants were asked to click in one of these areas to indicate where they felt their sense of self was located at that moment (state), and this click was recorded as a point in the body outline.
In this study, identification of self-location in the heart was scored as +1, and self-location in the head was scored as zero.

Self-construal was measured with (a) the Independent and Interdependent Self-Construal Scale (SCS; Kitayama et al., 2014; Singelis, 1994) and (b) the Metapersonal Self (MPS; DeCicco & Stroink, 2007) scale.
text.formatted: Self-construal was measured with (a) the Independent and Interdependent Self-Construal Scale (SCS; <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Kitayama et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Singelis, 1994)</ref> and (b) the Metapersonal Self (MPS; DeCicco & Stroink, 2007) scale.

text.text: The SCS assessed individuals' self-image as either independent (separate and unique) or interdependent (interpersonally connected), using a 7-point Likert scale.
The Independent subscale showed satisfactory reliability (α = .80; 15 items), while the Interdependent subscale demonstrated good reliability (α = .86; 15 items).
The MPS measured the extent to which individuals identify with an expansive, relationally connected self-construal, also using a 7-point Likert scale (α = .87; 10 items).

Self-concept was evaluated with the Self-Expansiveness Level Form (SELF) (Friedman, 1983), which quantifies self-concept expansion in time and space using a 5-point Likert scale across three levels: personal (α = .81; 5 items), middle (α = .87; 8 items), and transpersonal (α = .83; 5 items).

text.text: Dimensions of connectedness were measured using the Watts Connectedness Scale (WCS) and the Inclusion of Other in the Self (IOS) Scale.

The WCS (Watts et al., 2022) assessed felt connectedness using a 0-100 sliding scale across three dimensions: connection to self (α = .80; 6 items), others (α = .71; 6 items), and world (α = .86; 7 items).

text.text: The IOS (Aron et al., 1992) used seven Venn-like diagrams to measure the degree of perceived overlap between self and other, ranging from simple juxtaposition to complete overlap, in three different relationship contexts: intimate partner, close family, and friends (α = .67; 3 items).

text.text: Qualities of Connection were measured using the Qualities of Connection Measure (QCM), a single-item instrument developed specifically, using a 5-point Likert scale to assess the perceived presence of respect, appreciation, warmth, and heartfelt qualities in the experience of connection with others.
We a priori categorized respect and appreciation as cognitive and rational tendencies, and warmth and heartfelt feelings as somatic and interoceptive tendencies.
The question was: "When connecting with others, how much do you experience each of these qualities?
Cronbach's alpha was .88 with 4 items.
We employed a quantitative, cross-sectional, quasi-experimental design.
The study used a between-subjects design, stratifying participants into two groups (Head-locators and Heartlocators) based on their scores on the Dispositional Self-Location Questionnaire (DSLQ).
Recruitment was conducted both via Qualtrics® and personal social networks.

Participants were informed that the study would examine the nature of a strong feeling of connection with others (as in emotional connection, rather than erotic or sexual touch connection) and investigate what it means to engage with the world from a state of connectedness.
No indication was given in the recruitment materials or during the survey process that the study was investigating self-location.
All candidates were directed to the Qualtrics platform for selection.
To create a clear boundary and select individuals situated distinctly in one of the two zones, while excluding more ambiguous respondents, we eliminated those scoring between -5 and +5 on the DSLQ.

The 105 candidates who scored a minimum of +5 on the DSLQ constituted the primary group (Heart-located), whereas the 105 candidates who scored a minimum of -5 constituted the comparison group (Head-located).
The recruitment process was repeated with incremental selections until the primary and comparison groups were matched by gender, age, and level of education.
The selected candidates were then invited to complete the study measures.
The final Heart group consisted of 115 participants (105 from Qualtrics, 10 from social networks), and the Head group consisted of 103 participants (all from Qualtrics).

A power analysis using the G*Power app determined the sample size, indicating that two groups of 105 participants each would require an effect size of Cohen's d = 0.5, thereby allowing the use of p-values in hypothesis testing.
SPSS v.27 was used for data analyses.

The SELF, MPS, SCS, WCS, IOS, and QCM assessments were subjected to Pearson correlations and one-way ANOVA (i.e., t-tests), which allowed us to control for other variables (e.g., age, education) and assess validity.

False Discovery Rate (FDR)-adjusted Benjamini-Hochberg p-value at a q < .05 level of false discovery rate-was applied post hoc to control for the elevated risk of type I error rates associated with conducting multiple comparisons.

text.text: The FDR is reported as q-value.
The SP Body Map was analyzed by performing a chi-square test.
A post hoc ANOVA test was performed for analysis of the nine qualities of connection included in the DSLQ.

Our analytical approach prioritizes effect sizes and confidence intervals over sole reliance on p-values, reflecting our view that the practical significance of group differences is as important as their statistical significance.

text.text: These results support all three sub-hypotheses of Hypothesis 5, suggesting that warmth and heartfelt feelings tend to be more somatic and interoceptive than cognitive and rational.

text.text: Markedly, gender distributions varied significantly across these qualities, at times challenging conventional assumptions.

For instance, the study found more females than males in decisionmaking and knowing within the head location, whereas more males than females were found in caring, closeness, and empathy within the head location.

In summary, heart self-locators -validated by body map placement -reported significantly higher metapersonal self-construal, greater connectedness to self and world, and stronger warmth and heartfelt qualities of connection than head self-locators, while the two groups did not differ on independent self-construal, self-expansiveness, rational connection qualities, or interpersonal inclusion.
The primary aim of this study was to assess whether the somatic location of the selfhead versus heart-predicts the felt sense of connection (Gendlin, 2000; Yaden et al., 2017).

text.text: This study robustly supports two distinct somatic phenomenological profiles: head-locators inclined toward strong interpersonal boundaries and a rational focus, and heart-locators with preference for felt connection and emotional warmth.
The DSLQ's triangulation with body maps supports the notion that head-location and heart-location are lived experiences, not mere metaphors.
Head-locators did not report any lack of interpersonal connection, scoring similarly to heart-locators on Respect and Appreciation on the QCM.
However, their mode of relating relies more on higher-order cognitive processes rather than felt emotions.

Lower scores on MPS suggest that head-locators maintain a firmer distinction between self and other, viewing relationships as interactions between separate entities rather than in a field of shared experience.
The validation of the DSLQ through the body map and the post-hoc analysis of the qualities of decision-making and knowing reinforces the validity of this group's unique characterization.
The experiential functioning of the self, for head-locators, is likened to that of a control center, prioritizing accuracy and individuality over the diffusion of boundaries.
Heart-locators frequently indicated having the experience of a felt sense of connection, particularly characterized by warmth and heartfelt qualities.

The robust correlation with the MPS scale (q < .001) suggests that heart-locators tend toward the metapersonal self-construal: a stable self-understanding in which the self is experienced as profoundly interconnected with all humanity and nature (DeCicco & Stroink, 2007).

text.text: This is not merely a broader form of interdependence.
The interdependent self-construal remains anchored in interpersonal relations-the self as connected to close others.

The metapersonal self, by contrast, extends the relational field to include connection to the natural world and to life as a whole, or life itself, without requiring the spiritual or mystical framing that constructs such as universality orientation presuppose (Cloninger et al., 1994).

text.text: Equally, it should be distinguished from self-transcendence as a temporary experiential state (Yaden et al., 2017): the MPS captures a dispositional way of construing the self, not a transient peak experience.

text.text: This distinction is theoretically important because mainstream social psychology has predominantly defined connection as interpersonal (Aron & Aron, 1996), and even literature that acknowledges connection beyond the interpersonal tends to marginalize it, broadly labeling such connections "spiritual" or similar (Baumeister & Leary, 1995).

text.text: The present finding that heart-locators score significantly higher on MPS-while not differing from head-locators on the interdependent subscale-suggests that heart-based selflocation may specifically facilitate this broader, metapersonal mode of relating rather than merely intensifying interpersonal closeness.
Therefore, it can be considered that heart-locators do not just experience themselves as socially interdependent as much as deeply interwoven with the fabric of the world.
This is consistent with their higher scores on the Watts "Connection to
World" subscale but not necessarily on the IOS "Friends" subscale.
Their connection may be understood as a state of being characterized by warmth and authenticity rather than a social accumulation of friends.
The qualitative experience of connection reported by heart-locators appears to be situated in what Gendlin (2018) called the felt sense: a bodily knowing that precedes language.

It may be that self-location in the heart area facilitates interoceptive connection with the chest, a region rich in interoceptive afferents associated with emotional safety and bonding, thereby prioritizing access to pre-reflective experiences of relatedness.

This is consistent with the view that selflocation is an attentional stance that enhances access to specific cognitive resources: head-location facilitates separation and distinction, while heart-location prioritizes connection through a softening of self-other boundaries.
These results invite a theoretical comparison with neuroscientific accounts of the temporo-parietal junction (TPJ) and default mode network.
We advance the following interpretation as a hypothesis for future empirical validation, as no neural data were collected in the present study.
As noted by Blanke (2012) and Ionta et al. (2011), the TPJ mediates between "egocentric" (self) and "allocentric" (other) perspectives through multisensory integration.
text.formatted: As noted by <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Blanke (2012)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Ionta et al. (2011)</ref>, the TPJ mediates between "egocentric" (self) and "allocentric" (other) perspectives through multisensory integration.

text.text: Simultaneously, as noted by Babo-Rebelo and colleagues (2016), heartbeat-evoked responses that correlate with the sense of self ("I" and "me") modulate cognitive awareness in the default network.
The distinct profiles observed in our study suggest that heart-locators are likely prioritizing a different set of psychological resources than head-locators.

If the TPJ modulation can shift self-location, and if self-location correlates with connectedness, then the felt sense of connection may represent a complex interweaving of psychological traits and distinct neurophysiological states.

The head stance may represent a TPJ-mediated egocentric mode required for analytical tasks, whereas the heart-located state may represent a down-regulation of the boundary-enforcing mechanisms typically associated with the head-located perspective.
Whether these proposed correspondences between self-location profiles and neural mechanisms hold will require targeted neuroimaging or neuromodulation designs in future work.

The word "heart," when referring to lived experience, seems not merely a symbol used to designate some abstract or poetic idea but, for some individuals, is strongly associated with a self-sensation located in the upper torso.
Expressions such as "living from the heart" appear to be rather more than a metaphor.

The physical organ of the heart appears capable of responding to and participating in these localized sensations (Loescher et al., 2025; Yount et al., 2021), but the neurophysiology of subjectivity is a new research area, and no study has yet demonstrated a clear link.

text.text: Several limitations should be noted.

First, the cross-sectional, correlational design precludes causal inference; it is unclear whether heart-location causes connection, or whether highly connected individuals tend to situate their attention in the heart area.
Second, all measures relied on self-report, including the DSLQ, and no behavioral or physiological validation was conducted.
Physiological boundary dissolution, for instance, was not measured.
The DSLQ's convergent and discriminant validity-particularly against established interoception measures- has not yet been established.

Post hoc analysis showing that even heart-locators most often attribute decision-making to the brain suggests that participants possess a nuanced, non-binary understanding of their own functioning, supporting prior findings on the flexibility of temporary self-location in contextual situations.

Third, the sample was entirely American and recruited through purposive sampling of individuals who reported having experienced an intense sense of connection, which may have favored those more oriented toward relationality, even among the subsample of individuals who self-identified as being in the head.
Recruiting the heart-located group was notably faster than the head-located group, perhaps because those with a heart-located self may have greater interest in the study of interpersonal connection.
Head-located females aged 55-65 required the greatest effort to recruit.
These patterns may reflect sample bias.
The targeting was appropriate for our exploratory study, but cultural generalizability is therefore limited.
Fourth, although participants were deliberately kept unaware that the study examined self-location, reducing demand characteristics, these cannot be fully eliminated in a self-report design.

Finally, these findings require replication with new samples drawn from diverse populations (e.g., various cultural and ethnic groups, meditators, neurodivergent individuals), particularly given the U.S. purposive sample, as well as stability reports.
Several directions follow from these limitations.
Neurophenomenological measures (e.g., extrapersonal space testing) could assess physiological boundary dissolution, using meditators able to accurately report associated self-location.

Longitudinal studies should test the efficacy of these findings over time and across situations to verify the extent of dispositional self-location and context-specific responses, and further studies should investigate the modifiability of these states.
Based on the present data, two main adjustments to the DSLQ are anticipated.

The option "liver" should be replaced with "gut," which corresponds to distinct somatic intuitions, and certain items reworded to reduce potential semantic associations (e.g., in item #2, the contrasting choice to "interpersonally warm" should become "interpersonally reserved" rather than "interpersonally cold"; Sester, 2024).
The focus on head and heart, although empirically grounded and supported by participant responses with multiple choices and/or availability across all body regions, should continue to be challenged.
Similarly, the cultural meanings of body organs or regions vary across history and geography, requiring careful examination.
Transcultural validations are needed.
On the clinical level, learning to shift the source of attention toward the chest may help restore a sense of connection in individuals who suffer from social anxiety.

More broadly, stepping out of the head-and its tendencies toward control-may help broaden the range of adaptive responses and emotional intelligence and open access to meaning by touching what goes beyond the ego and the rational.
This study provides empirical evidence that supports the notion that the located sense of self in the body relates to how individuals engage with the world.
The head self-location fosters a sense of individuality, rationality, and boundary-setting as necessity.

Somatic self-location centered in the heart area seems likely to foster the warm, expansive felt sense of connection described by poets, mystics, and lovers, a moving transpersonal experience of connection that bridges the gap between self and other.
